opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to what kind of generalization you actually want. If you look at how deep learning works, you're fitting a parametric curve via gradient descent, and that gives you a continuous, interpolative model. It's very good at value-centric abstraction, recognizing that two things are similar in some embedding space. But it's quite poor at program-centric abstraction, at discovering discrete structure that you can reuse and recombine in a principled way.

When you search over program graphs, you're building solutions out of discrete, composable pieces. A program you discover that way tends to generalize much more strongly, because it captures the actual underlying rule rather than a smooth approximation of examples. If you find the right program for a task, it'll work on inputs far outside the distribution you saw, which is something a curve fit generally can't give you.

The reason I emphasize *iterative* search is that pure brute-force program synthesis runs into combinatorial explosion almost immediately. The space of possible programs is astronomically large. So you can't just enumerate. What you want is a process that incrementally builds up a library of useful building blocks, reusable abstractions, and then searches over compositions of those. Each time you solve something, you extract what was reusable and add it to your library, so the next search becomes shallower. That's how you get efficiency over time. It mirrors how humans seem to work: we're not re-deriving everything from scratch, we're recombining concepts we've already mastered.

And I don't think it's either/or with deep learning. The most promising direction, in my view, is to use deep learning as a kind of intuition engine to guide the discrete search: to tell you which branches of the program graph look promising, so you don't have to explore everything. Deep learning gives you fast, approximate pattern-matching, what you might call System 1, and discrete program search gives you the precise, verifiable reasoning, more like System 2. Intelligence, to me, is really about the efficiency with which you can turn limited experience into new skills, and that kind of hybrid is how you get there.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the core of it is that I think intelligence is fundamentally about program synthesis. When you're faced with a new problem, something you haven't seen before, what you're really doing is assembling a new program on the fly out of building blocks you already have. And the question is, how do you search for that program?

The space of possible programs is combinatorial, it's enormous. So you cannot enumerate it. You need some form of guided search, and crucially, you need the search to be iterative. You don't get the right program in one shot. You propose something, you run it, you look at where it fails, and you use that feedback to refine the next candidate. That loop, propose, verify, revise, is the heart of it.

Now, why program graphs specifically? Because programs have structure. They're not flat strings. If you represent them as graphs, where nodes are operations and edges are data flow, then you can do very targeted edits. You can swap one operator, re-route one input, splice in a subgraph that worked on a related problem. The search becomes local in a meaningful sense. A small change in the graph is a small change in behavior, mostly, which is not true if you're editing text token by token.

And there's a deeper reason, which is that this is where I think deep learning and discrete search complement each other. Deep learning is extremely good at intuition, at perception, at pattern recognition. It's bad at precise, compositional, combinatorial reasoning. Search over program graphs gives you that rigor. But unguided search is hopeless, so you use a learned model to guide it, to propose which edits are promising, to prune the space. The model provides the intuition, the search provides the guarantees. You get something that can actually generalize to genuinely novel tasks, which is what ARC is designed to test, rather than just interpolating between things it's memorized.

So that's the bet. Intelligence is the efficiency with which you can turn experience into new programs, and iterative search over structured program representations is, I think, the most direct way to build that.

r001.rationale: The response says graph representations allow targeted edits such as swapping operators or rerouting inputs, and contrasts this with editing text token by token.

r002.rationale: It describes programs as structured rather than flat strings and represents that structure with graph nodes for operations and edges for data flow.

astra-6.text:
Because when you’re trying to solve a new problem, you generally can’t produce the right program in one shot. You have a partial understanding of what’s needed. You try something, you look at what it does, and you use that feedback to revise your hypothesis. That iterative process is central to how I think about program synthesis.

A program graph gives you a structured space in which to do that. You can compose existing pieces, change one part while preserving the rest, or abstract a useful subprogram so you can reuse it. You’re searching over explicit computational structures that you can execute and test.

Of course, the space of programs is enormous. So the point isn’t to do blind search. You want learned intuition to guide it: which components are likely to be useful, which modifications are promising, which hypotheses are worth testing. Deep learning can provide those priors, while execution gives you feedback grounded in what the program actually does.

What appeals to me is that combination: intuition proposes something, and a structured process tests and refines it. You can spend more computation on a genuinely new problem instead of depending entirely on whether a solution was already captured during training.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because a program has a very natural compositional structure. You have pieces that implement useful functions, and you can combine those pieces into something more complex. If you represent this as a graph, you can search by making local changes: replacing a component, adding a connection, or reusing a subprogram you’ve already discovered.

The important thing is that you don’t have to get the whole program right in one shot. You propose something, evaluate it against the task, and use that feedback to guide the next proposal. Of course, the search space is enormous, so you need strong priors to make that process tractable. Learning can provide those priors: it can suggest which components or modifications are likely to be useful.

So I see learning and search as complementary. Learning gives you intuition about where to look, and explicit program execution lets you test whether what you found actually works.
